title: The $100 Startup
subtitle: Reinvent the Way You Make a Living, Do What You Love, and Create a New Future
author: Chris Guillebeau
why_it_matters: It made a case that business writing had mostly ignored: a profitable company can be one person, a laptop and a few hundred pounds, and that is a legitimate destination rather than a stepping stone to something bigger.

crux.headline: A business is something useful, sold to someone who wants it
crux.body: Most people overbuild before they earn anything. The smaller path is to find the narrow overlap between what you can already do and what somebody will pay to have done, describe it as a change in their life rather than a list of features, and charge money for it this month. Revenue is the only permission you need. The entity, the branding and the plan can all be assembled afterwards, out of money customers have already handed over.

sparks.hook: Your hobby is not a business until it solves someone else's problem.
sparks.insight: Passion on its own does not pay. Neither does a dull but profitable service you cannot stand to deliver. The businesses that work for one person sit in the narrow band where something you are genuinely good at meets a problem other people already want solved and will hand over money to be rid of. Test the overlap by describing your idea entirely from the buyer's side: what is different about their week after they pay you? If you cannot answer that without talking about yourself, you have a hobby with an invoice attached.
sparks.why: Enthusiasm gets you through the unpaid months, but only demand produces revenue. The overlap is narrower than most people assume, which is why so many passion projects stall at exactly the point where money should start appearing.
sparks.apply: Write your idea as one sentence describing what changes for the customer, with no mention of you, your credentials or your process. Show it to three people who might pay.

sparks.hook: Nobody wants your product. They want the version of their life that comes after it.
sparks.insight: Every feature you are proud of is a detail of how the thing works. Buyers care about what changes. A course is not forty video lessons; it is the job you get afterwards. A booking tool is not a calendar; it is never again losing an evening to messages about scheduling. Translating features into outcomes is not spin, because if you cannot name the outcome you are probably selling something nobody needed. Write the outcome first, then let it decide which features are worth building at all.
sparks.why: Purchases are made against an imagined future state, not against a specification. Outcome language also exposes weak ideas early: a product with no describable after is usually a product with no buyer waiting for it.
sparks.apply: Take your product page or pitch and rewrite every feature line as the difference it makes to the customer's day. Delete any feature that has no such line.

sparks.hook: You could be open for business by the end of the week, and probably should be.
sparks.insight: The apparatus most people assemble before their first sale, the company and the logo and the website and the plan, teaches you nothing about whether anyone wants what you have. Selling teaches you that in a day. A working microbusiness needs only four things: a product or service, a group of people who want it, a way for them to pay, and a way to deliver. Everything else is decoration that can be bought later out of profit. Start with the smallest arrangement that can legally take money.
sparks.why: The expensive part of a bad idea is the months you spend preparing to test it. Selling early converts an argument you cannot win inside your own head into a fact you can act on. It is cheap to be wrong quickly.
sparks.apply: Name the smallest version of your offer that somebody could buy this week, then set up one payment link for it before you build anything else.

carousel.title: Name the offer
carousel.body: Decide exactly what someone receives and what it costs. One product, one price, one type of buyer. Ambiguity at this stage shows up later as an empty inbox you cannot explain.

carousel.title: Find fifty people
carousel.body: Locate a group that already has this problem and already gathers somewhere: a forum, a newsletter, a local trade association. You need access to fifty of them, not an audience of thousands.

carousel.title: Take money first
carousel.body: Set up the simplest possible way to be paid before you finish building. A payment link and an honest delivery date is enough to learn whether the offer is real.

carousel.title: Deliver by hand
carousel.body: Fulfil the first orders manually, even though it does not scale. The friction you feel doing it yourself is the specification for whatever you automate next.

sparks.hook: Bootstrapping is not a virtue. It is a way of keeping every decision yours.
sparks.insight: Money you did not raise cannot be taken back, and nobody attached to it gets a say in what you build. A business funded by its own sales grows at the speed of demand, which is slower and far more honest than growth funded by somebody else's expectations. The trade is real: you will be smaller, and you will pass on opportunities that need capital. What you get is a company that can be profitable at your size, rather than one that must keep getting bigger to survive the terms of its own funding.
sparks.why: Outside money changes the required outcome, not just the runway. A business that needs a large exit cannot choose to stay small, even in cases where staying small is exactly what would make its owner well off.
sparks.apply: Work out the monthly revenue that would cover your living costs plus a modest buffer, and treat that number as your first target instead of a growth rate.

sparks.hook: Ask people what they are struggling with before you decide what to build.
sparks.insight: The cheapest research available is a direct question to the people you hope to serve, asked before you have anything to defend. What is the most frustrating part of this for you? What have you already tried? What would you pay to never deal with again? Answers arrive in the customer's own words, which is useful twice: once to shape the product, and once to write the sales page, because language that came from buyers converts better than language invented by the seller.
sparks.why: Asking before building keeps you from falling in love with a solution. It also gathers phrasing you could not have invented yourself, since customers describe their problems in terms no product team would ever choose.
sparks.apply: Send five short questions to twenty people in your target group this week. Ask about their problem rather than your idea, and record their exact phrasing.

sparks.hook: An offer that is always available gives nobody a reason to buy today.
sparks.insight: Interest decays fast. Someone enthusiastic about your offer on Tuesday will have forgotten by Friday unless something forces a decision. That is why launches, closing dates, limited runs and price changes work: not because they manipulate people, but because they replace a vague someday with a specific choice. The line to watch is honesty. If the deadline is invented and then quietly extended, you have taught your audience that nothing you say about timing is true, and you only get to do that once.
sparks.why: Deferred decisions are usually abandoned decisions. Constraints raise conversion because they collapse an open question into a yes or a no, but they keep working only while the constraint is genuine.
sparks.apply: Give your next offer a real closing date or a real limit, put it in writing to your list, and hold it exactly as stated even if the sales are slower than you hoped.

sparks.hook: The asset is not the product. It is the list of people who trust you.
sparks.insight: Products age, platforms change their rules, and search rankings move without warning. A direct line to people who have said they want to hear from you survives all of that, and it is the one thing a small business can own outright. Every launch should add names to that line, and every piece of free work you publish should have somewhere for interested people to land. Size matters less than relationship: a few hundred people who actually open your messages will out-earn a large following that ignores you.
sparks.why: Rented audiences vanish when an algorithm changes. Owned contact lists keep working, and response rate matters more than headcount, because revenue comes from the people who reply rather than the people who follow.
sparks.apply: Add one obvious way to join your list to the piece of free content that already gets the most traffic, then email that list something useful within a fortnight.

carousel.title: Give something away
carousel.body: Publish the most useful thing you can make in an afternoon and let people have it without payment. Usefulness earns the address. A signup form on its own does not.

carousel.title: Write like a person
carousel.body: Send messages a single reader would want to receive: short, specific, occasionally about something other than selling. A broadcast tone trains people to skim past you.

carousel.title: Sell without apology
carousel.body: When you do have something to sell, say so plainly and explain who it is for. People who joined because you were useful are not offended by an offer, only by a disguise.

sparks.hook: Charge for the result, not for the hours it happened to take you.
sparks.insight: Time-based pricing punishes you for getting better. The faster and more skilled you become, the less you earn for the same outcome, which is a strange incentive to build a business on. Pricing against the value of the result breaks that link: what matters is what the work is worth to the buyer, not how long it sat on your calendar. This is easier for small operators than they expect, because the person buying rarely wants your hours. They want the thing to be handled.
sparks.why: Hourly rates cap earnings at the number of hours you can survive. Value pricing is not always available, though, and works best where the outcome is measurable and the buyer is a business rather than a person spending their own money.
sparks.apply: Take one service you currently sell by the hour and rewrite it as a fixed-price package with a defined deliverable, then offer that version to the next enquiry.

sparks.hook: Most small businesses fail quietly, and case studies rarely include them.
sparks.insight: Books assembled from success stories are built backwards: someone found people who made it work, then looked for what they had in common. The failures who did the same things are not in the room. That does not make the advice useless, but it changes how you should use it. Treat every case study as one route that existed under particular conditions, a specific market, a specific year, a founder with savings or a partner's income or an existing audience, rather than a formula that transfers reliably to your situation.
sparks.why: This is survivorship bias, and it is the central weakness of founder literature. The honest reading is that these methods improve your odds inside a favourable setup, not that following them produces the same outcome.
sparks.apply: For any case study that inspires you, write down three conditions the founder had that you do not, and decide how you would cover each one before starting.

sparks.hook: You do not need a business plan. You need to know who pays and why.
sparks.insight: Long plans are written for people who were never going to fund you anyway. A one-person business can hold its entire strategy on a single sheet: what you sell, who buys it, how they find out, how they pay, what delivery costs you, and what has to be true for the numbers to work. Writing it small has a useful side effect. Vagueness that survives in twenty pages is impossible to hide in six lines, so the exercise finds your weakest assumption before the market does.
sparks.why: The value of planning is the thinking, not the document. Short formats force you to state assumptions explicitly, which is what makes them testable rather than merely reassuring to read back.
sparks.apply: Fill one page with six headings: offer, buyer, channel, payment, costs, and the assumption most likely to be wrong. Then go and test that last one first.

actions: Pick the single skill you already have that someone has paid you for, or nearly paid you for, and turn it into one clearly priced offer this week.
Interview ten people in your target market about their problem before building anything, and write down the phrases they use so you can sell in their words.
Set up a payment link and make one real sale, however small, before spending money on branding, incorporation or a website.
Calculate the monthly revenue that would cover your living costs, and track progress against that number rather than against followers or traffic.
not_for_you_if: You are building something that needs a factory, a research lab or venture funding, or you want rigorous evidence rather than a collection of encouraging case studies.

verification.notes: First published 2012 by Crown Business. All prose here is original; case studies are described in general terms and no figures or wording from the book are reproduced.

title: Rework
author: Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson
why_it_matters: It gave a generation of small software companies permission to stay small, profitable and unfunded, and argued it in short blunt chapters that were impossible to skim past. Much of the modern bootstrapped software scene traces its attitude back here.

crux.headline: Constraints are not obstacles. They are the strategy
crux.body: Most of what looks like running a company is theatre: forecasts nobody can honestly make, meetings that produce agreement instead of output, headcount hired to signal seriousness. Strip that away and what remains is a small group making something people will pay for and getting it in front of them. Fewer people, fewer features and less money force decisions that a well-funded team is able to avoid making, and those forced decisions are usually the right ones.

sparks.hook: A long-term plan is a guess wearing a suit.
sparks.insight: A three-year plan requires you to know things you cannot know: what the market will want then, what competitors will do, who will still work for you. Writing it anyway does not create knowledge. It creates commitment to a guess, and commitment is expensive, because you will defend the plan long after reality has contradicted it. Deciding in shorter horizons keeps you responsive. You still choose a direction. You just stop pretending the choices two years out can be made accurately today.
sparks.why: Forecast accuracy collapses as the horizon lengthens, and written plans create anchoring: teams keep executing a strategy because it is documented, not because the evidence still supports it.
sparks.apply: Replace your next annual roadmap with a written list of what you will build in the coming six weeks, and hold everything beyond that as options rather than commitments.

sparks.hook: Working eighty hours is not dedication. It is usually bad prioritisation.
sparks.insight: Long hours look like commitment and often signal the opposite: unclear priorities, an inability to decide what not to do, or a culture that rewards visible effort over finished work. Tired people make worse decisions, then spend the next day fixing them, which produces more hours and more mistakes. The person who leaves at six having shipped something has done more than the one who stayed until midnight rewriting a proposal that was going to be cut anyway.
sparks.why: Sustained overwork degrades judgement and creativity well before it degrades the volume of output, so the hours keep rising while useful work falls. The honest caveat is that some phases genuinely do demand a sprint.
sparks.apply: For one week, track what you actually finished each day rather than hours worked, then cut the two activities that consumed the most time for the least result.

sparks.hook: When you run out of money, time or people, you start making real choices.
sparks.insight: Abundance lets you avoid deciding. With enough budget you can build every feature anyone asked for, hire around every problem, and postpone the question of what the product is actually for. Scarcity removes that option. A team of three cannot ship twelve things, so it has to know which one matters, and that knowledge is the most valuable thing a young company can own. Treat your limits as the filter that produces focus rather than as the reason you cannot compete.
sparks.why: Constraints force prioritisation, which is the skill most associated with small teams beating larger ones. The caveat: some markets genuinely require capital, and no amount of focus substitutes for it.
sparks.apply: List everything on your build queue, then choose what you would ship if you had one third of your current time and budget. Ship exactly that, and nothing else.

sparks.hook: Cut the scope, never the standard of whatever survives the cut.
sparks.insight: When a project runs late, the instinct is to keep every feature and lower the quality of all of them. That produces something nobody enjoys using. The better move is to remove whole features and finish the rest properly. Users forgive a product that does three things well and does not attempt a fourth; they abandon one that does nine things badly. Deciding what to drop is uncomfortable, because somebody asked for each item, but the alternative is shipping a compromise nobody asked for at all.
sparks.why: Perceived quality is driven by the worst parts of an experience rather than the average. Removing weak features raises the standard of the whole product without any additional building.
sparks.apply: Take your current feature list and delete the bottom half by importance. Ship the top half finished, and wait to see who complains before restoring anything.

carousel.title: List everything promised
carousel.body: Write down every feature currently in scope, including the ones added quietly in meetings. You cannot cut what is not visible on a single page in front of you.

carousel.title: Rank by who leaves
carousel.body: Order the list by which absences would actually cost you a paying customer. Most items turn out to be preferences rather than requirements once you ask that question.

carousel.title: Cut, do not shrink
carousel.body: Remove whole items rather than shipping thin versions of all of them. Half a good feature is a support ticket waiting to be filed against you.

carousel.title: Finish what remains
carousel.body: Spend the reclaimed time making the survivors genuinely good, including the boring edges: error states, empty screens, and what the second visit feels like.

sparks.hook: A meeting costs the number of people in the room times its length.
sparks.insight: An hour with eight people is a working day gone, and most of it buys agreement rather than output. Meetings are also fragmenting: the half hour before one is rarely used for anything demanding, so the real cost is larger than the calendar shows. This does not mean never gather. It means treating a meeting as an expensive tool with one specific job, a decision that genuinely needs several people present, and refusing to use it for status updates that could simply be read.
sparks.why: Concentrated work requires long uninterrupted blocks, and a scheduled interruption fragments the time on both sides of it. The cost is the lost depth, not only the hour marked on the calendar.
sparks.apply: Cancel one recurring meeting this week and replace it with a written update. Reinstate it only if something measurably breaks within the following month.

sparks.hook: Teach people how you do the work. Nobody copies it well enough to matter.
sparks.insight: Small companies worry that publishing their methods hands an advantage to competitors. In practice, showing your reasoning attracts the people who want to buy from someone who thinks that way, and rivals who copy the surface rarely copy the judgement underneath it. Teaching is also a cheaper channel than advertising: it costs your knowledge rather than your budget, and it compounds, because useful material keeps working long after a campaign has finished spending its money.
sparks.why: Explaining your process builds trust faster than claims about yourself, since a reader can evaluate the thinking directly. It works best in fields where expertise is the product, and is weaker for commodity goods.
sparks.apply: Publish one honest write-up of how you solved a real problem this month, including what you got wrong, and put it where your customers already read things.

sparks.hook: Hire only after the work has been genuinely painful for a while.
sparks.insight: Adding a person is often a way of avoiding a decision about what not to do. The discipline is to feel the pain of the missing role long enough to understand it precisely: what the job actually involves, on your real workload, rather than the idealised version. Doing the work yourself first also means you can tell whether the new hire is good at it. Companies that hire ahead of need end up manufacturing work to justify the headcount, and that work becomes permanent.
sparks.why: Roles defined before the need is felt tend to describe an imagined job. Waiting produces a sharper specification and a better test of candidates, at the cost of a stretch of real strain on whoever is covering.
sparks.apply: Before opening a role, do that job yourself for two weeks and write down each task you performed. Hire against that list rather than against a generic job title.

sparks.hook: Every yes to a customer request is a no to something you cannot see.
sparks.insight: Feature requests arrive with a face attached, so refusing feels rude, while the cost of accepting is invisible: the maintenance, the settings screen that keeps growing, the future customers confused by a product that no longer has a clear shape. Saying no politely and often is how a product keeps its identity. You are not telling customers they are wrong. You are telling them what your product is for, which is information they need in order to decide whether it is for them.
sparks.why: Accepted requests accumulate permanent complexity while their benefit is usually limited to the person who asked. Clear refusal also reduces churn from mismatched users who would have left later, and angrier.
sparks.apply: Write a short standard reply explaining what your product deliberately does not do, and send it the next time a request falls outside that boundary.

carousel.title: Assume no first
carousel.body: Treat any request as declined until it repeats from several customers who are paying you. Enthusiasm from one loud user is not evidence of demand from the rest.

carousel.title: Explain the shape
carousel.body: Refuse by describing what the product is for, rather than by promising to consider it later. Vague deferral generates follow-up questions and false hope.

carousel.title: Keep the count
carousel.body: Log every refusal. When one request appears again and again from your best customers, that record is what tells you the answer should now change.

sparks.hook: Culture is what you repeatedly tolerate, not what you wrote on a wall.
sparks.insight: You cannot install a culture by announcing values. What people learn is behavioural: who got promoted, which corner-cutting went unmentioned, whether the person who worked all weekend was praised for it. Those signals accumulate into the real rules of the place, and they will beat any poster that disagrees with them. Young companies often defer culture until they are bigger, but by then it has already formed out of whatever the founders happened to do while they were busy.
sparks.why: Norms propagate through observed behaviour and consequences rather than through stated intentions. That is why values documents written after the fact usually describe a company that no longer exists.
sparks.apply: List the last three behaviours you rewarded and the last three you let pass. That pair, not your values page, is your current culture. Change one of the six.

sparks.hook: One profitable company is not a controlled experiment.
sparks.insight: The strongest objection to advice from any successful small company is that it is a single case, written by the people who won with it. Staying unfunded worked for a software business with low costs, an early audience and a product it could sell directly to individuals. Those conditions do not transfer to a hardware company, a marketplace that needs both sides at once, or anyone without savings to fall back on. Read the reasoning, which usually survives. Be careful with the prescriptions, which often do not.
sparks.why: A sample of one cannot separate the method from the circumstances. The useful test is whether the mechanism behind a piece of advice still makes sense in your market, not whether it worked in theirs.
sparks.apply: For each rule you plan to adopt, write down the condition that made it work for its author, then check honestly whether that condition holds for you.

actions: Cancel or shorten every recurring meeting on your calendar for two weeks, and note which ones anyone actually asks to bring back afterwards.
Cut your current project's scope in half by removing whole features, then finish what remains to a standard you would happily show a stranger.
Write and publish one detailed account of how your team solved a real problem, mistakes included, and send it to your customer list.
Replace your annual plan with a six-week list of committed work, and review what changed at the end of it rather than at year end.
not_for_you_if: You run or plan a capital-intensive business, or you want evidence and nuance rather than confident short arguments delivered with very little hedging.

title: Shoe Dog
subtitle: A Memoir by the Creator of Nike
author: Phil Knight
why_it_matters: Most founder memoirs are written to look inevitable in hindsight. This one keeps the fear in: years of near-insolvency, a bank that wanted rid of the company, and decisions made without knowing. It is the honest version of how a famous brand got built.

crux.headline: Growth and cash are not the same thing
crux.body: A company can double its sales every year and still be days away from collapse, because growth consumes cash before it produces any. The story behind one of the world's best-known brands is mostly a story of that gap: ordering more inventory than the balance sheet justified, paying suppliers before customers paid, and persuading somebody each year to fund the difference. The product mattered, but survival came down to who kept lending.

sparks.hook: You can triple your sales every year and still nearly die of it.
sparks.insight: Growth is expensive before it is profitable. You buy stock, ship it, wait to be paid, and by the time the money arrives you have already ordered more. Sales that double each year double the size of that hole. Companies in this position are not failing. They are succeeding in a way that consumes cash faster than it generates it, and the only question is whether somebody will fund the gap until the cycle turns. Plenty of good businesses die here while their revenue chart still points upward.
sparks.why: This is the working capital cycle, and it kills more growing companies than weak demand does. Profit on paper and cash in the bank account can move in opposite directions for years at a time.
sparks.apply: Model the next twelve months as cash in and cash out by week, rather than as revenue by quarter, and find the exact week where the balance turns negative.

carousel.title: Map the cycle
carousel.body: Write down the number of days between paying your supplier and being paid by your customer. That figure, multiplied by your growth, is the hole you have to fund.

carousel.title: Shorten both ends
carousel.body: Ask for longer terms from suppliers and shorter terms from customers. A fortnight at each end can be worth more to a small company than a funding round.

carousel.title: Fund the gap early
carousel.body: Arrange the credit line while the numbers still look good. Money is offered to companies that do not yet need it and withdrawn from the ones that do.

carousel.title: Cap the order
carousel.body: Set a maximum order size you could survive not selling. Growth beyond that limit is a bet on demand, and it should be a deliberate bet rather than a habit.

sparks.hook: Conservative bankers are not villains. They are just not your partner.
sparks.insight: A lender's upside is being repaid. It does not share in the company that gets built. So a bank looking at a business with thin reserves and aggressive orders sees risk with no compensating reward, and behaves accordingly, whatever it said when the relationship began. Founders take this personally and should not. The practical lesson is to know what each source of money is actually optimising for before you depend on it, and to line up an alternative long before the current one gets nervous.
sparks.why: Debt providers have capped upside and full downside exposure, so their incentives diverge from yours at precisely the moment you are growing fastest and need them most.
sparks.apply: List every source of money keeping you alive, write down what each one gets if you succeed, and open a conversation with one alternative source this quarter.

sparks.hook: The supplier who made you can also decide to replace you.
sparks.insight: Building a business on somebody else's product means the relationship is the business. Distribution agreements get renegotiated, manufacturers notice how much you are selling and start wondering why they need you, and every improvement you make to the market makes taking it back more attractive. Depending on a single partner is a workable way to start and a dangerous way to stay. The decision that matters is when to begin building your own version, which will always feel both too early and too expensive.
sparks.why: Value migrates towards whoever controls the scarce part of the chain. A distributor's leverage falls as the market it created becomes obvious and easy for the manufacturer to serve directly.
sparks.apply: Name the single partner whose withdrawal would end your business, then spend this quarter building the smallest possible independent alternative to them.

sparks.hook: The first order was placed by a graduate with no company and no money.
sparks.insight: The start was closer to improvisation than strategy. A business school paper about importing running shoes from Japan turned into a trip, then a meeting arranged with more confidence than credentials, then a company name invented on the spot when a manufacturer asked who he represented. The first stock was small, funded by a loan from family, and sold out of a car at track meets. None of it was a plan. It was a series of moves small enough to make without permission, each one creating the conditions for the next.
sparks.why: Early progress often comes from actions that are cheap to take and hard to reverse rather than from planning. The uncomfortable part is that this method also produces many failures, and nobody wrote a memoir about those.
sparks.apply: Identify the one move you could make this month that requires nobody's approval and would force a real answer from the market. Make it before you plan any further.

carousel.title: Ask for the meeting
carousel.body: The unreasonable request costs a letter and a plane ticket. Most people never make it, which is why the ones who do end up meeting suppliers who had no reason to say yes.

carousel.title: Buy the smallest batch
carousel.body: Order the least you can that still proves the idea. Small orders are fundable by people who love you and survivable in the case where nobody buys.

carousel.title: Sell where they gather
carousel.body: Go in person to the places your buyers already are, and let them handle the product. Credibility comes from being one of them, not from advertising at them.

carousel.title: Reinvest all of it
carousel.body: Put the proceeds straight into the next, larger order and repeat. The compounding is real, and so is the widening cash gap that it opens underneath you.

sparks.hook: Hire people who annoy you slightly and argue with each other loudly.
sparks.insight: The early team was not assembled for polish. It included an accountant who had struggled to hold a job elsewhere, a couple of former athletes, people with obvious flaws and one unusual strength each. What held them together was loyalty to the thing being built and a willingness to say plainly that an idea was bad. Companies that hire for smoothness get agreement, and agreement is worthless when nobody knows the answer. Early on you want a small group who will fight in the room and then execute together.
sparks.why: Diverse thinking improves decisions under uncertainty, but only where disagreement is safe to voice. The failure mode is confusing tolerance for dysfunction with tolerance for difficult but capable people.
sparks.apply: In your next contentious decision, ask the person most likely to disagree to argue the opposing case first, before anyone senior has stated a preference.

sparks.hook: The product got better because a coach kept ruining kitchen equipment.
sparks.insight: The technical advantage did not come out of a laboratory. It came from a track coach who had been cutting up and rebuilding shoes for his own athletes for years, chasing a few grams of weight and a better grip, and who eventually poured rubber into a household waffle iron to see what pattern it produced. Real product insight tends to come from someone who uses the thing obsessively and is irritated by it, rather than from a market study. Find that person and then get out of their way.
sparks.why: Users at the extreme end of a use case notice problems earlier and describe them more precisely than average users do. Their improvised fixes are crude, but they point directly at the real constraint.
sparks.apply: Find the most obsessive user of your product, spend an hour watching them work, and build the fix they have already improvised for themselves in some awkward way.

sparks.hook: A brand is a promise you keep for years before anybody notices it.
sparks.insight: The name, the logo and the slogans arrived later and more cheaply than people assume, and none of them created the brand. What created it was a decade of selling to serious runners, backing athletes nobody had heard of yet, and being present at the events where credibility is granted rather than bought. Identity accumulates from consistent behaviour in front of a specific group. Marketing can accelerate that once it exists, but marketing applied to a company with no record only makes the emptiness legible faster.
sparks.why: Brand equity is built from repeated, consistent experience with a defined audience. Advertising amplifies an existing reputation far more reliably than it manufactures one from nothing.
sparks.apply: Pick one specific group whose respect would matter most to your customers, and do something genuinely useful for that group every month for a year.

sparks.hook: Going public was treated as a defeat, not as a celebration.
sparks.insight: Selling shares to the public solved a cash problem that had run for close to two decades, and it also ended something: the ability to decide without explaining, to invest through a bad year, to keep the company's business private. Founders who chase a listing as the finish line are often chasing the moment their choices stop being entirely their own. That may still be the right trade, particularly when the alternative is running permanently short of money. But it is a trade, not a prize.
sparks.why: Public markets supply capital in exchange for disclosure, quarterly scrutiny and a legal duty to shareholders. That constraint is real and, in practice, close to irreversible.
sparks.apply: Before pursuing any funding event, write down which decisions you will no longer be able to make alone afterwards, and check that you can live with that list.

sparks.hook: The memoir is honest about the price, which founder stories rarely are.
sparks.insight: Alongside the growth there is a marriage strained by permanent absence, sons who saw a father who was mostly not there, and decades of anxiety that the company would not survive the month. The account does not resolve this into a tidy lesson about balance, because it was not balanced. That refusal is the most useful part of it. Ambition at this scale costs something specific and non-refundable, and the version of the story that leaves the cost out is the version that gets people into trouble.
sparks.why: Founder narratives usually edit out the personal damage because it complicates the moral. Naming it is not discouragement. It is the information you need in order to choose knowingly.
sparks.apply: Write down what you are prepared to give up over the next three years, and what you are not. Share the second list with the people it directly affects.

sparks.hook: For every founder who survived running out of cash, several did not.
sparks.insight: The habit of ordering more stock than the balance sheet supports, betting the company on a single supplier relationship, and staying permanently one bad month from insolvency reads as courage here because it worked. Run that same strategy a thousand times in the same era and most attempts end in liquidation, with no memoir attached. The transferable parts are the specific ones: understand your cash cycle, know who funds the gap, own the scarce link in your chain. The aggression is not a method.
sparks.why: Only the winners publish. Extreme risk-taking looks like conviction from inside a success and like recklessness from inside a failure, and the two are indistinguishable while the outcome is still open.
sparks.apply: Before copying a bold move from a founder story, work out what that same decision would have cost you had the market moved against it, and size the bet accordingly.

actions: Build a weekly cash forecast for the next six months and mark the week your balance turns negative. Fix that week before chasing more sales.
Identify the supplier, lender or platform whose withdrawal would end you, and start building a second option this quarter even if it costs more.
Choose one community whose respect your customers care about, and show up in it consistently for a year with something useful rather than promotional.
Write down the personal cost you are willing to pay over the next three years, and discuss it with the people who will pay part of it alongside you.
not_for_you_if: You want a repeatable framework or management advice. This is a memoir told by the winner, offering atmosphere and hard-won detail rather than method.

verification.notes: First published 2016 by Scribner. Prose is original; events are described in general terms and no figures or sentences from the memoir are reproduced.

title: The Mom Test
subtitle: How to Talk to Customers and Learn if Your Business is a Good Idea When Everyone is Lying to You
author: Rob Fitzpatrick
why_it_matters: It fixed the most common failure in early-stage building: founders running conversations that generate encouragement instead of evidence. Short, blunt, and still the standard reference for asking questions that can actually prove you wrong.

crux.headline: Ask about their life, never about your idea
crux.body: People lie to you in customer conversations, mostly out of kindness. They praise the idea, agree it is a problem, and promise to buy, because that is what politeness sounds like. The fix is not better wording but a different subject: stop discussing the thing you want to build and ask what they actually did the last time the problem occurred, what it cost them, and what they have already paid to fix it. Facts about the past are the only answers that carry information.

sparks.hook: A good meeting where nobody commits to anything is a bad meeting.
sparks.insight: The most dangerous outcome of a customer conversation is warmth. You leave energised, they said it sounded interesting, everybody smiled, and nothing about your situation has changed. Enthusiasm is free to give, so it tells you nothing. The only signals with weight are the ones that cost the other person something: time booked in a diary, money, or their reputation staked on an introduction to a colleague. Judge every conversation by what was given up, not by how it felt on the way out.
sparks.why: Verbal support has no cost, so it does not discriminate between people who will buy and people who are being kind. Costly signals do, which is why commitment is the only reliable early measurement available to you.
sparks.apply: End your next customer conversation by asking for something concrete: a follow-up with their manager, a paid trial, or a date in the diary. Record what they actually gave.

sparks.hook: Compliments are the sound of a conversation failing politely.
sparks.insight: When somebody says your idea is great, the interview has already gone wrong. They are being nice, which is the socially correct thing to do, and you have just spent the meeting talking rather than learning. The repair is to stop presenting entirely. Ask what they currently do about the problem, when it last happened, and what they did about it then. If the compliment arrives anyway, deflect it and return to their life, because praise is the least informative thing a potential customer can offer you.
sparks.why: Politeness norms make encouragement the default response to any pitch, which is why enthusiastic feedback correlates poorly with later purchasing. The information is in behaviour, not in approval.
sparks.apply: In your next three conversations, do not describe what you are building until the final two minutes. Spend the rest of the time asking how they handle the problem now.

sparks.hook: Stop asking what people want. Ask what they already did about it.
sparks.insight: Predictions about future behaviour are unreliable even when the person is trying hard to be honest, because nobody has good access to what they will do under conditions that have not happened yet. Their past is different. It is a record, not a guess. So the useful questions all point backwards: when did this last bite you, what did you do, how long did it take, what did you spend, who else was involved. Everything you learn that way is a fact, and facts survive contact with your business plan.
sparks.why: Stated preferences and revealed preferences diverge widely, especially for hypothetical purchases. Past behaviour is the closest thing to evidence you can obtain before you have a product to sell.
sparks.apply: Rewrite your interview script so that every question refers to something that has already happened, and delete anything containing the word would.

carousel.title: Narrow the segment
carousel.body: Keep splitting your target group until you can name where these people are and what they have in common. A segment you cannot find is a segment you cannot test.

carousel.title: Open with their day
carousel.body: Start with how the work actually happens now, step by step. You are mapping a routine, and the pain will show up inside it without you having to name it.

carousel.title: Find the last time
carousel.body: Ask when the problem last occurred and walk through it in detail. Specific incidents produce specific answers; general questions produce general noise.

carousel.title: Price the pain
carousel.body: Ask what it cost them: hours, money, a lost client, an argument with a colleague. A problem with no measurable cost is one nobody will pay to remove.

carousel.title: Ask for a step
carousel.body: Close by requesting something real: an introduction, a deposit, a scheduled trial. Their answer will tell you more than the previous half hour did.

sparks.hook: Asking someone whether they would buy this is close to useless.
sparks.insight: Asked directly, most people say yes. Refusing a hopeful founder feels unkind, and imagining a purchase is nothing like making one. The question also invites the other person to speculate about a version of themselves who does not exist yet. Replace it with questions about now: what are you using, what did it cost, how did you choose it, what would have to be true for you to switch. If you want a real answer about whether they will buy, offer to take their money today.
sparks.why: Hypothetical purchase intent overstates real demand, because the imagined transaction carries no budget, no approval process and no competing uses for the money attached to it.
sparks.apply: Replace every would-you question in your script with a what-do-you-currently question, then test the real one by asking for a pre-order or a deposit.

sparks.hook: The more formal the meeting, the worse the information you get.
sparks.insight: A scheduled interview with a slide deck puts the other person into a role: reviewer, adviser, polite audience. They start giving feedback on your presentation instead of describing their life. Casual conversations produce better data because nobody is performing. Ask your questions over coffee, in a corridor, in a message thread. You are not running a study. You are finding out how somebody actually works, and people describe that most accurately when they do not feel they are being surveyed.
sparks.why: Framing a conversation as an evaluation shifts the other person into critique mode, which produces opinions about your idea rather than descriptions of their behaviour. Informality lowers that pressure.
sparks.apply: Have your next three learning conversations without a deck, a demo or a scheduled slot. Keep the questions in your head and write the answers down straight afterwards.

sparks.hook: Find out who signs, or you are selling to someone who cannot buy.
sparks.insight: Enthusiasm from the person who feels the problem is not the same as a purchase, because in most organisations they are not the one who releases money. Part of every early conversation should map the machinery: who owns this budget, what does a purchase of this size require, who has stopped a similar decision before, and how long did the last comparable purchase take. Founders who skip this spend months delighting a champion who was never able to say yes on their own.
sparks.why: Buying processes contain several distinct roles: the user, the budget holder, and whoever can veto. Selling to only one of them is the most common way a promising pipeline stalls without any clear explanation.
sparks.apply: In your next sales conversation, ask how the last purchase of this kind was approved, who was involved, and how long it took from first meeting to payment.

sparks.hook: If you cannot describe how you might be wrong, you are not testing.
sparks.insight: Most founders enter customer conversations wanting to hear that the idea is good, and they get what they came for, because questions can be shaped to produce almost any answer. The discipline is to write down beforehand the specific belief you are checking and what evidence would count against it. Three questions per conversation is enough. If none of them could produce an answer you would find disappointing, you are collecting encouragement rather than information, and encouragement does not survive launch day.
sparks.why: Confirmation bias operates through question selection more than through interpretation. Pre-committing to a disconfirming test is the standard defence, and it works in commercial settings as well as scientific ones.
sparks.apply: Before your next conversation, write the three questions you most fear the answer to. Ask those first, while you still have the other person's full attention.

sparks.hook: Three kinds of answer sound useful and contain nothing at all.
sparks.insight: Bad data is dangerous because it feels like progress. Compliments are praise for you rather than facts about them. Fluff is anything hypothetical, general or about the future: what they usually do, what they would do, what they intend to do next year. Feature requests are the customer doing your job badly, guessing at a solution instead of describing the problem underneath it. Each has a repair, and running the repair turns a wasted meeting into a useful one without starting again.
sparks.why: These three categories cover most of what founders bring back from customer conversations. Naming them makes the failure visible in the moment, which is the only time it can actually be corrected.
sparks.apply: Read your last set of interview notes and mark each line as fact or non-fact. If most of the page is non-fact, rerun those conversations with better questions.

carousel.title: Deflect the praise
carousel.body: When someone compliments the idea, thank them briefly and immediately ask what they currently do instead. Praise is the moment to change subject, not to relax.

carousel.title: Anchor the fluff
carousel.body: When an answer is general or hypothetical, pull it into a specific event: when did that last happen, what did you do, and what did it cost you that day.

carousel.title: Dig under the request
carousel.body: When they ask for a feature, ask why they want it and what they are doing about it now. The reason is real data; the requested feature usually is not.

sparks.hook: Everyone is not a segment. Neither is small businesses.
sparks.insight: A group defined too broadly gives you contradictory answers, because you are averaging across people with different problems. Keep slicing until the segment shares a job, a workflow and a reason to care: not runners, but people training for a first marathon on a coached plan. The test of a good segment is practical. You should be able to say where to find twenty of them this week. If you cannot, the segment is a description rather than a market, and your interviews will keep producing noise.
sparks.why: Aggregating dissimilar users hides the signal, since strong demand in a narrow group looks like weak demand across a broad one. Narrow segments also make early distribution tractable rather than theoretical.
sparks.apply: Take your current target market and split it three times, until you can name a specific place where twenty of these people could be reached this week.

sparks.hook: The notes you did not write down are the ones you will invent later.
sparks.insight: Memory reconstructs conversations in a way that favours whatever you already believed. Within a day an ambiguous answer becomes supportive and a hesitation becomes enthusiasm, and there is no way to notice this from the inside. Write down what people said in their own words, as close to verbatim as you can manage, and mark clearly which parts are quotation and which are your interpretation. That record is what lets you and your co-founder argue about evidence instead of about recollections.
sparks.why: Reconstructive memory reliably drifts towards prior belief, and the drift is invisible to the person doing it. Contemporaneous notes are the cheapest correction available to a small team.
sparks.apply: Write up each customer conversation within an hour, separating what they said from what you concluded, and share both with whoever else makes product decisions.

actions: Book five conversations with people in one narrow segment and run all of them without describing what you are building until the final minutes.
Rewrite your interview script so every question is about something that has already happened, and delete anything hypothetical.
Ask for a real commitment at the end of every conversation, then track who gave time, money or an introduction and who gave only praise.
Map the buying process for your product: who uses it, who pays, who can veto, and how long the last comparable purchase took.
not_for_you_if: You already have paying customers and a working sales process, or you want a broad startup manual rather than one narrow discipline done properly.

verification.notes: First published 2013, self-published by the author. Prose here is original; the framework is described in our own words with no wording reproduced.

title: Founders at Work
subtitle: Stories of Startups' Early Days
author: Jessica Livingston
why_it_matters: It captured what early-stage companies looked like before the retelling smoothed them out, in the founders' own recollections. Decades on it is still the best antidote to the tidy origin story, and a record of how much of technology began by accident.

crux.headline: Almost nothing started as the thing it became
crux.body: Read enough founding accounts side by side and the pattern is not vision. It is adaptation. Companies began as something else, ran out of money, were rejected by investors who later looked foolish, and survived because a small group refused to stop and stayed alert enough to notice which part of their work people actually used. The consistent trait across these interviews is not brilliance or timing. It is a willingness to keep going while being wrong in public.

sparks.hook: The famous product is usually the third idea, not the first one.
sparks.insight: Read a dozen founding accounts in a row and the same shape keeps appearing. A team sets out to build one thing, discovers that a side feature is the only part anyone uses, and rebuilds the company around it. A photo-sharing service grew out of an online game. A payments company went through several products before finding the one that stuck. The original idea was rarely the asset. What mattered was still being solvent and paying attention when the real one appeared.
sparks.why: Early markets cannot be predicted from outside them, so a first idea functions mainly as a way of getting close enough to see the real one. That only helps if you survive long enough to look.
sparks.apply: Look through your usage data for the feature people use in a way you did not intend, then spend a week treating that behaviour as though it were the whole product.

sparks.hook: The trait these founders share is stubbornness, not intelligence.
sparks.insight: Across very different people and decades, the recurring quality is not raw brilliance. Plenty of clever people leave when the work stops being fun. What repeats is an unreasonable refusal to stop: continuing after the funding round collapsed, after the launch nobody noticed, after a co-founder walked out. This is not inspirational filler, it is a selection effect with teeth. Startups take longer than expected and fail quietly rather than dramatically, so the main way to lose is to run out of willingness before you run out of options.
sparks.why: Persistence is genuinely necessary, though the honest caveat is that it is nowhere near sufficient. Stubbornness also keeps founders on doomed ideas, and these interviews include only people whose stubbornness was eventually rewarded.
sparks.apply: Write down in advance what evidence would make you stop and what would make you continue. Decide it now, while you are calm, rather than during a bad month.

sparks.hook: Investors who passed on these companies had good reasons at the time.
sparks.insight: Almost every founder here describes being turned down, often by people who understood the industry well. The idea sounded small, the market did not exist yet, the founders were young and had no record. Rejection is not evidence that you are right, but it is not evidence that you are wrong either. Investors pattern-match against companies that already worked, which by definition cannot include anything genuinely new. Take the specific objections seriously and treat the verdict itself as one opinion.
sparks.why: Early-stage judgement is poor because the reference class is missing. The same reasoning that produced famous misses also correctly rejects the far larger number of ideas that really do fail.
sparks.apply: After your next rejection, write down the objection rather than the outcome, and decide which objections are answerable with evidence you could gather this month.

sparks.hook: The first users were recruited one at a time, usually by the founder.
sparks.insight: None of these companies began with a growth strategy. Someone emailed a list of friends, posted to a forum they already belonged to, demonstrated the thing at a meeting, or added a quiet line to every outgoing message inviting the recipient to try it. Early distribution is manual and unglamorous, and that is the point: doing it by hand teaches you who your users are and why they stay, which is the only knowledge that later makes a real growth channel work.
sparks.why: Manual acquisition does not scale, but it produces high-resolution information about motivation and objection. Automating before you have that information tends to scale the wrong message very efficiently.
sparks.apply: Personally recruit the next twenty users yourself, one conversation at a time, and record the exact sentence that persuaded each of them to try it.

carousel.title: Go where they already are
carousel.body: Use the communities, mailing lists and events you or your users already belong to. Borrowed trust is the cheapest distribution a company with no reputation can get.

carousel.title: Invite people by name
carousel.body: Send individual messages rather than announcements. A personal request converts far better and produces a reply you can actually learn something from.

carousel.title: Watch the first use
carousel.body: Sit with new users while they try it. The place they hesitate is your real roadmap, and you will not see it from an analytics dashboard afterwards.

carousel.title: Build in the invitation
carousel.body: Once people stay, make sharing a natural part of using the product rather than a separate campaign. Growth that lives inside the product keeps working.

sparks.hook: Not knowing it was impossible was frequently an advantage.
sparks.insight: Several of these founders were young, underqualified or working outside their field, and built things that experienced people had decided could not be done cheaply. Inexperience is genuinely costly in most respects, but it removes one specific handicap: knowing every reason a similar approach failed before. That knowledge is usually correct and occasionally out of date, because the underlying costs changed while nobody was looking. The newcomer's advantage is not intelligence. It is being unaware of a constraint that has quietly expired.
sparks.why: Expert judgement encodes the conditions under which the expertise was formed. When those conditions change, the encoded rule keeps producing confident answers that are no longer accurate.
sparks.apply: Name one thing everyone in your field agrees is not worth trying, then check whether the reason it failed still holds given current costs and available tools.

sparks.hook: Every company here nearly died, and most of them more than once.
sparks.insight: The tidy version of a startup story skips the month when payroll was uncertain, the servers that stayed down through a launch, the losses growing faster than revenue, the co-founder who left. In these accounts those episodes are the substance of the early years. It is worth knowing before you start, because when your own crisis arrives you will assume it means the company is not working. Usually it means the company is at the stage where crises are the normal weather.
sparks.why: Founders judge their situation against published narratives that omit the bad months, so an ordinary crisis reads as a fatal verdict. Better reference points reduce the number of companies abandoned unnecessarily.
sparks.apply: Ask two founders one stage ahead of you what went wrong in their first two years, and specifically what nearly ended it. Write down what you hear, verbatim.

sparks.hook: Ship while you are still embarrassed, then fix it in public.
sparks.insight: Repeatedly in these accounts, the product that won was released before it was ready, sometimes to a small invited group and sometimes to anyone who arrived. What early release buys is not speed for its own sake. It replaces a private argument about what users want with a public record of what they did. The cost is real: a rough launch can burn a reputation with a specific audience, so the skill is choosing an audience that will forgive roughness in exchange for being early.
sparks.why: Feedback quality rises sharply once real users are involved, because usage exposes assumptions that discussion cannot. The caveat is that a poor first impression is expensive in markets where trust is itself the product.
sparks.apply: Pick the smallest audience that would tolerate a rough version, and put your current work in front of them this month rather than after the next milestone.

carousel.title: Choose a forgiving group
carousel.body: Release first to people who want the problem solved badly enough to tolerate rough edges. Early adopters trade patience for influence over what you build next.

carousel.title: Instrument the basics
carousel.body: Know who arrived, what they tried, and where they stopped. Without that record you will hear opinions afterwards and still not know what actually happened.

carousel.title: Fix in the open
carousel.body: Publish what you are changing and why. Visible responsiveness converts a bad first impression into evidence that the product is being taken seriously.

sparks.hook: Co-founder trouble ends more companies than competitors ever do.
sparks.insight: These interviews are full of partnerships that carried a company through years of difficulty, and of splits that nearly ended one. What separates them is rarely talent. It is whether the hard conversations were held early: who decides when you disagree, what happens to equity if somebody leaves in year two, what each person is actually committing to. Those discussions feel unnecessary while everyone is excited, which is exactly when they are cheap to have and still possible to hold honestly.
sparks.why: Founder disputes usually arise from expectations that were never made explicit rather than from bad faith. Written agreements made early are easier precisely because nothing valuable is yet at stake.
sparks.apply: Agree in writing with your co-founder this month: decision rights, vesting, what counts as full-time, and how either of you can leave without destroying the company.

sparks.hook: These interviews are a list of winners with the losers left out.
sparks.insight: Every person here built something that worked, which means the collection cannot tell you which behaviours caused success. Thousands of founders were equally persistent, launched equally early and pivoted equally boldly, and their companies closed anyway. What a collection like this is genuinely good for is expanding your sense of what is normal: how messy the start is, how much changes, how ordinary the people are. Use it to calibrate expectations, not to derive a formula for outcomes.
sparks.why: With no failure cases in the sample, no causal claim can be supported. Interview collections are useful as descriptions of the range of experience, not as evidence about what reliably works.
sparks.apply: For every lesson you take from a founder story, ask what a founder who did the same thing and failed would have written. If you cannot tell them apart, treat it as unproven.

sparks.hook: Being underestimated is a resource you spend down as you grow.
sparks.insight: Several of these companies operated for years while larger incumbents ignored them, and that inattention was worth more than any feature. A small team serving a market that looks too small to matter is left alone to learn, and by the time the opportunity is obvious it has accumulated years of specific knowledge. The window closes. Once you are visible, competitors copy quickly, so the question worth asking early is what you can build during obscurity that stays hard to copy afterwards.
sparks.why: Incumbents allocate attention to defensible revenue, which makes small or awkward markets genuinely invisible for a period. That period is finite, and it tends to end without much warning.
sparks.apply: Write down what you will have built by the time competitors notice you: data, relationships, distribution, or a hard technical component. Then work on that first.

actions: Read three founding accounts back to back and list what each company changed between its first idea and the one that eventually worked.
Recruit your next twenty users personally, one conversation at a time, and record the sentence that persuaded each of them to try it.
Write down now what evidence would tell you to stop and what would tell you to keep going, so the decision is not made during a bad month.
Settle decision rights, vesting and exit terms with your co-founder in writing while the company is still worth very little.
not_for_you_if: You want a framework or a step-by-step method. This is oral history: long interviews, mostly American technology companies, and no attempt at a general theory.

verification.notes: First published 2007 by Apress. All prose here is original; the interviews are characterised in general terms and no wording from them is reproduced.

title: The Personal MBA
subtitle: Master the Art of Business
author: Josh Kaufman
why_it_matters: It argues that the useful content of a business degree is a set of mental models you can learn in a year of reading, then supplies them in one volume. As a map of how any company actually functions it has no obvious rival at this length.

crux.headline: Every business does the same five things
crux.body: Strip away the industry and every company runs the same loop: it creates something people want, gets those people to notice it, persuades enough of them to pay, delivers what was promised, and takes in more money than it spends doing so. If any one of the five is missing you have a project rather than a business. Most confusion about strategy dissolves once you can say which of the five is currently broken.

sparks.hook: A business is five processes. Yours is failing at one of them.
sparks.insight: Value creation, attention, persuasion, delivery, and money left over. Every company that survives does all five, and every company in trouble can usually name the one that has stopped working. This is more useful than it sounds, because founders tend to fix whichever part they enjoy. Engineers rebuild the product when the real problem is that nobody knows it exists. Marketers buy more traffic when delivery is so poor that customers leave anyway. Diagnose first and the correct work is usually obvious.
sparks.why: The five-part model is descriptive rather than predictive, but it works well as a checklist. Most persistent business problems turn out to be a single broken stage that was quietly being compensated for elsewhere.
sparks.apply: Score each of the five stages of your business from one to ten this week, then spend the following month working only on the lowest one.

carousel.title: Create something wanted
carousel.body: Make a thing that solves a problem people already have. If nobody has the problem, no amount of skill further down the chain can rescue it.

carousel.title: Earn attention
carousel.body: Get in front of people likely to want it. Attention is a separate discipline from building, and it does not arrive automatically because the product is good.

carousel.title: Convert to payment
carousel.body: Turn interest into a transaction by removing the specific reasons this buyer would hesitate. Interest that never becomes payment is a cost, not an asset.

carousel.title: Deliver reliably
carousel.body: Provide what was promised at a standard that produces repeat business. Delivery failures are the most expensive kind, since you already paid to acquire that customer.

carousel.title: Keep a margin
carousel.body: Take in more than you spend, with enough left to survive a bad quarter. Revenue without margin only accelerates the arrival of the problem.

sparks.hook: No market, no business. Everything else is a detail.
sparks.insight: The most common startup failure is not bad execution. It is building something skilfully for a group of people who do not want it badly enough to pay. Nothing downstream repairs this: better design, lower pricing, harder selling, all of it fails against an absent market. So the first question is never how to build the thing. It is whether a group of people already have this problem urgently, can be reached, and have money. Answering badly wastes years; answering early costs a few weeks.
sparks.why: Demand is the binding constraint most of the time. Execution quality matters enormously, but only within a market that exists, which is why market selection outranks nearly every other early decision.
sparks.apply: Before building further, write down where your buyers gather, how urgent the problem is, and what they currently spend on it. Any blank is a research task for this week.

sparks.hook: There are only about a dozen ways to charge for anything.
sparks.insight: Under the surface, business models repeat: sell a product, sell your time, rent shared access, charge a recurring fee, buy and resell, lease an asset, take a cut as an agent, gather an audience and sell its attention, lend money, sell an option, insure against a risk, or invest capital for a share. Knowing the list is practical, because many stuck businesses are simply running the wrong one. The same underlying value can often be delivered under a model that fits your costs far better.
sparks.why: The number of distinct ways value gets exchanged is small and stable across industries. Treating the model as a variable rather than a given opens options that product changes cannot reach.
sparks.apply: Write down your current model, then describe how you would deliver the same value as a subscription, as a shared resource, and as an agency. Cost each one roughly.

sparks.hook: Value is not in the thing. It is in what the buyer already wants.
sparks.insight: Nothing has value on its own. A product is worth what it does for a particular person given what they are already trying to achieve: to acquire something, to belong, to understand, to protect what they have, or to feel differently. Two customers can pay wildly different amounts for an identical item because the underlying drive differs. This is why arguing that your product is objectively good rarely moves anyone. You are not raising the quality. You are failing to connect it to a motive that already exists.
sparks.why: Value is subjective and contextual, which is standard economics rather than a novel claim. The practical consequence is that positioning against an existing motive beats improving the specification.
sparks.apply: For your main product, write down which human motive it serves most directly, then rewrite your headline so that motive appears in the first six words.

sparks.hook: You can grow revenue in only four ways. Pick one deliberately.
sparks.insight: Serve more customers, make each purchase larger, get people to buy more often, or charge more per unit. That is the whole list, and each option carries a different cost. Acquiring new customers is usually the most expensive and the most popular, because it feels like growth. Raising prices is the cheapest and the most feared. Increasing purchase frequency often requires the least new work of all, since the relationship and the delivery system already exist and the customers already trust you.
sparks.why: The four levers are arithmetically exhaustive for revenue. They differ enormously in marginal cost, so choosing the wrong one is the difference between profitable growth and expensive growth.
sparks.apply: Estimate what a ten percent gain would cost you through each of the four levers, then pursue only the cheapest one for the next quarter.

sparks.hook: The price is a decision you make, not a fact you discover.
sparks.insight: Most small businesses price by looking at competitors, which imports somebody else's cost structure and somebody else's mistakes. Other anchors are available. What would it cost this buyer to solve the problem another way, or to do nothing? What is the measurable financial gain from your work? Prices are also information: too low and buyers assume poor quality, too high and you attract customers expecting more support than they pay for. Choose the anchor consciously, then test it rather than defending it.
sparks.why: Price is one of the few variables that moves straight to profit, since raising it costs almost nothing to implement. It is also the variable founders adjust least often, usually out of fear.
sparks.apply: Raise the price of one offer by twenty percent for the next ten enquiries, and record what actually happens to your conversion rate before deciding anything.

carousel.title: Cost of replacement
carousel.body: Work out what it would cost the buyer to build or arrange this themselves, including their own time. That figure sets a rough ceiling on any discount.

carousel.title: Compare the market
carousel.body: Look at what similar things sell for, but treat it as a reference point rather than an instruction. Your competitors are guessing about price too.

carousel.title: Estimate the gain
carousel.body: Where the outcome is financial, estimate what your work is worth to the buyer over a year, then price as a defensible fraction of that number.

carousel.title: Test, do not agonise
carousel.body: Change the price and watch behaviour for a fixed period. Ten real enquiries tell you more than a month of internal debate ever will.

sparks.hook: Profit is an opinion. Cash in the account is a fact.
sparks.insight: A business can report profit while running out of money, because profit counts sales you have made and cash counts money you have actually received. The gap between them fills with unpaid invoices, stock sitting in a warehouse, and expenses paid in advance. Owners who watch only the profit line get ambushed by a payroll they cannot meet during their best quarter. Watching cash weekly is unglamorous, and it is the single financial habit most likely to keep a small business alive.
sparks.why: Accrual accounting recognises revenue when it is earned rather than when it is received. That is useful for measuring performance and actively dangerous as a guide to solvency.
sparks.apply: Set up a simple weekly view of money in, money out and the closing balance, and look at it every Monday before you look at any other number.

sparks.hook: Improving anything except the bottleneck improves nothing at all.
sparks.insight: Every system has one constraint that sets its total output, and work spent anywhere else just piles up inventory in front of it. A studio that can sell ten projects a month but deliver six is not helped by better marketing. A production line moves at the speed of its slowest station. The discipline is to find the constraint honestly, improve it until it moves somewhere else, then repeat. Most efficiency effort in small companies goes instead to whichever part was easiest to optimise.
sparks.why: This is the theory of constraints, and it holds for any system with sequential dependencies. The counter-intuitive part is that local improvements away from the bottleneck can make overall performance worse.
sparks.apply: Draw your delivery process as a sequence of stages with a capacity number on each. Find the smallest number and spend the next month on that stage alone.

sparks.hook: Automating a broken process gives you the same mess, faster.
sparks.insight: Software applied to a process nobody understands produces errors at a higher rate and hides them behind an interface. The order to work in is: do it manually until it is boring, write down the actual steps including the exceptions, simplify until several steps disappear, and only then automate what is left. Automation is also brittle in a way manual work is not. When it fails, the people who could have handled the exception have forgotten how, because the system was doing it for them.
sparks.why: Automation multiplies whatever the process already does, errors included. It also removes the practice that keeps human fallback capability alive, which is why the failures tend to arrive as surprises.
sparks.apply: Take the process you were about to automate and simplify it manually first. Remove two steps, then automate what remains and keep a written fallback procedure.

sparks.hook: Decide what enough looks like before the business decides for you.
sparks.insight: Companies expand to fill whatever ambition is available, and without a stated target the default is more of everything, indefinitely. Working out the number that would cover your costs, pay you properly and leave a buffer turns an open-ended race into a finite problem you can solve. It also changes decisions: once the target exists, an opportunity that doubles revenue and triples your working hours can be declined without it feeling like failure. Growth becomes a choice rather than an obligation.
sparks.why: Explicit targets convert vague ambition into a decision rule. Without one, every opportunity looks like a reason to expand, because there is no defined standard against which to decline it.
sparks.apply: Calculate the annual revenue and profit that would genuinely be enough for you, write it down, and use it to decline the next opportunity that misses it.

actions: Score each of the five stages of your business from one to ten, then spend the next month improving only the lowest-scoring stage.
Build a weekly cash view showing money in, money out and closing balance, and check it before any other number each Monday morning.
Map your delivery process stage by stage with a capacity figure on each, find the bottleneck, and work on nothing else until it moves.
Test a twenty percent price rise on one offer across your next ten enquiries and record the effect on conversion before deciding.
not_for_you_if: You want depth in one discipline, or you already run a business and know the fundamentals. It is deliberately broad, and each model gets only a few pages.

verification.notes: First published 2010 by Portfolio, with a revised edition later. All prose here is original and the models are described in our own words.

title: Company of One
subtitle: Why Staying Small Is the Next Big Thing for Business
author: Paul Jarvis
why_it_matters: It made questioning growth respectable. Rather than treating small as a phase to be escaped, it sets out why a deliberately capped business can be more resilient and more profitable per person than one built to keep expanding.

crux.headline: Growth is a choice, and usually an unexamined one
crux.body: Almost every business assumes bigger is the goal, then hires, borrows and takes on complexity in service of an outcome nobody actually chose. A company of one starts from the other end: decide what enough looks like in money and in hours, then build the smallest arrangement that reliably produces it. Everything past that number has to justify the cost it adds, because growth is not free and the bill arrives as complexity, overheads and lost autonomy.

sparks.hook: Ask what your business is for before you ask how big it should get.
sparks.insight: Growth is the default answer to every question in business, which means it is rarely an answer at all. More customers, more staff, more revenue: each brings costs that are easy to overlook while the top line rises. More people means management, coordination and payroll that must be met every month.
